question: Early years care is essential for the health of children with developmental disorders or at risk of developing them. Andalusia’s reform to its social care services is reorganising its schools and staffing, severing therapeutic relationships built up over many years, although Andalusia’s Early Care Act requires ongoing high-quality, child- and family-centred care.

Professionals with decades of experience are also being laid off, depriving children of expert care. This flies in the face of the rights enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, in particular the best interests of the child, the protection of health, inclusion and non-discrimination.

It also runs counter to the European Education Area’s objectives of removing barriers to learning. Stable, high-quality care at an early age is crucial for reducing difficulties and promoting inclusive education. 1.
What view does the Commission take of this complaint regarding early years care for children in Andalusia?
What does the Commission intend to do about this?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.11.2026) The Commission acknowledges the importance of providing quality education and care to young children and of safeguarding the stability and continuity of services for children with special educational needs, also by ensuring adequate working conditions and stability for the specialised professionals providing these services.

While the situation is under the responsibility of the Spanish regional and national authorities, the Commission encourages Member States to provide free and inclusive access to a set of essential services (such as early childhood education and care) to children in need through the Child Guarantee1.

The European Education Area Strategic Framework also supports access to high-quality early childhood education and care (ECEC), based on the European Quality Framework for ECEC2. The Commission supports implementation of this Framework through Erasmus+ funding, research and support to policy cooperation, for example with the Toolkit for inclusive ECEC3.

Furthermore, the Action Plan on Basic Skills4 foresees the publication in 2028 of ‘Guidelines for curriculum development in ECEC, which support the acquisition of basic skills early on and facilitate early detection and intervention of developmental delays.

These initiatives provide recommendations and practical suggestions to Member States to ensure that all children can receive the care and education they need in their early years. EU funding programmes such as the European Social Fund Plus5 or the European Regional Development Fund6 can also support regions to enhance the provision of quality education and care to all children.
